links.note: Greek coordinates Jesus and his disciples; English uses “with.”
“When” expresses the time relationship of the Greek participle.
Greek asks a verbless question, literally “What to me and to you?”
English repeats the relative object as “it.”
“Way of purifying” renders the Greek noun “purification.”
Greek says “up”; English specifies the brim.
Greek says “it is”; English expresses the wine’s origin with “came.”
The verb’s unnamed plural subject is identified as the guests.
Greek describes becoming drunk; English says “drunk freely.”
The shared possessive applies to both brothers and disciples.
Greek says “not many”; English says “a few.”
English introduces the subject before the participle; Greek carries it in the following finite verb.
English repeats the changers as possessors of the tables.
Greek says “a house of trade”; English contracts this to “a marketplace.”
English introduces elapsed time with “It took”; Greek simply says the temple was built in those years.
Greek says “had need”; English uses the verb “need.”
